Inflation

A finite ensemble Kalman filter underestimates its own uncertainty, and each analysis makes that worse. Once the spread is too small the gain shrinks, the observations stop mattering, and the error grows while the ensemble reports that all is well. Inflation puts spread back deliberately.

Three questions organise this chapter. Why does the spread come out too small, even with a perfect model? What does each inflator do to the covariance, and in particular to the correlations and the rank? And what can go wrong, given that an adaptive belief can freeze and an inflator can create spread that nothing removes? Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage appears at the end because it treats the same disease from a different side. It regularises a covariance estimate, and it does not touch the ensemble.

Why the spread comes out too small¶

Take one observed scalar, with forecast variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 and observation variance σε2\sigma_\varepsilon^2σε2​. The optimal analysis variance is v(σ2)v(\sigma^2)v(σ2), where

v(s)=s σε2s+σε2.v(s) = \frac{s \, \sigma_\varepsilon^2}{s + \sigma_\varepsilon^2}.v(s)=s+σε2​sσε2​​.
(12.1)

An ensemble only has the sample variance s^\hat{s}s^, with E[s^]=σ2\mathbb{E}[\hat{s}] = \sigma^2E[s^]=σ2, and sampling error acts in two directions. The variance the ensemble reports is v(s^)v(\hat{s})v(s^), and vvv is concave in sss, so by Jensen’s inequality the report is too low on average:

E[v(s^)]≤v(σ2).\mathbb{E}[v(\hat{s})] \le v(\sigma^2).E[v(s^)]≤v(σ2).
(12.2)

The error the analysis actually has comes from the gain g^=s^/(s^+σε2)\hat{g} = \hat{s} / (\hat{s} + \sigma_\varepsilon^2)g^​=s^/(s^+σε2​). The optimal gain minimises the following error, so a noisy gain can only add to it:

E[(1−g^)2σ2+g^2σε2]≥v(σ2).\mathbb{E}\left[(1 - \hat{g})^2 \sigma^2 + \hat{g}^2 \sigma_\varepsilon^2\right] \ge v(\sigma^2).E[(1−g^​)2σ2+g^​2σε2​]≥v(σ2).
(12.3)

So (12.2) and (12.3) pull apart even with a linear model and Gaussian noise. The ensemble reports less than the optimum, and it achieves more error than the optimum.

It prints 0.474 0.529, against an optimum of v(1)=0.5v(1) = 0.5v(1)=0.5. The ratio of the two is the spread deficit that an analysis starts from, before any model error or nonlinearity adds to it. Model error adds a second cause, since members that run through an imperfect model do not carry that model’s error in their spread.

Localization is sometimes listed as a third cause, but on a single analysis it acts the other way. In Program 12.2 the localized analysis keeps more spread than the unlocalized one, because the localized gain contracts each site less.

It prints 0.423, 0.459 and 0.492: the unlocalized analysis, the localized one, and the forecast they both start from.

Multiplicative inflation¶

The simplest fix scales the anomalies about the mean Anderson & Anderson, 1999. With factor ζ\zetaζ,

x(e)←xˉ+ζ(x(e)−xˉ),Σ^x←ζ2Σ^x.\vect{x}^{(e)} \leftarrow \bar{\vect{x}} + \zeta \left(\vect{x}^{(e)} - \bar{\vect{x}}\right), \qquad \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x \leftarrow \zeta^2 \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x.x(e)←xˉ+ζ(x(e)−xˉ),Σ^x​←ζ2Σ^x​.
(12.4)

It keeps the mean, every correlation and the span of the anomalies. The docstring gives ζ∈[1.01,1.10]\zeta \in [1.01, 1.10]ζ∈[1.01,1.10] as typical for operational numerical weather prediction. Applied uniformly, it boosts densely observed regions and data-void regions alike. A direction with no spread stays with no spread, since ζ⋅0=0\zeta \cdot 0 = 0ζ⋅0=0.

Relaxation: RTPS and RTPP¶

Relaxation methods blend the analysis with the forecast, so the correction is largest where the analysis contracted most. Write σi,t∣t\sigma_{i, t \mid t}σi,t∣t​ and σi,t∣t−1\sigma_{i, t \mid t-1}σi,t∣t−1​ for the analysis and forecast spread of component iii, and take α∈[0,1]\alpha \in [0, 1]α∈[0,1].

RTPS¶

Relaxation to prior spread Whitaker & Hamill, 2012 relaxes the spread of each component and rescales its anomalies to match:

σitarget=(1−α)σi,t∣t+ασi,t∣t−1,x~i(e)←κix~i(e),κi=(1−α)+ασi,t∣t−1σi,t∣t+ϵ,\sigma_i^\text{target} = (1 - \alpha) \sigma_{i, t \mid t} + \alpha \sigma_{i, t \mid t-1}, \qquad \tilde{x}^{(e)}_i \leftarrow \kappa_i \tilde{x}^{(e)}_{i}, \qquad \kappa_i = (1 - \alpha) + \alpha \frac{\sigma_{i, t \mid t-1}}{\sigma_{i, t \mid t} + \epsilon},σitarget​=(1−α)σi,t∣t​+ασi,t∣t−1​,x~i(e)​←κi​x~i(e)​,κi​=(1−α)+ασi,t∣t​+ϵσi,t∣t−1​​,
(12.5)

where x~i(e)\tilde{x}^{(e)}_ix~i(e)​ is the analysis anomaly and ϵ=10−12\epsilon = 10^{-12}ϵ=10−12 is an absolute floor set by gaussx. In matrix form the covariance becomes DΣ^x∣yD\mat{D} \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{x \mid y} \mat{D}DΣ^x∣y​D with D=diag(κ)\mat{D} = \op{diag}(\gvect{\kappa})D=diag(κ), and a two-sided diagonal scaling leaves every correlation unchanged. So RTPS adjusts the marginal spreads and keeps the correlation structure the analysis produced.

RTPP¶

Relaxation to prior perturbations Zhang et al., 2004 blends the anomaly matrices themselves:

X~t∣t←(1−α)X~t∣t+αX~t∣t−1.\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t} \leftarrow (1 - \alpha) \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t} + \alpha \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t-1}.X~t∣t​←(1−α)X~t∣t​+αX~t∣t−1​.
(12.6)

Its covariance contains the cross term between the two anomaly matrices,

(1−α)2Σ^x∣y+α2Σ^x+α(1−α)X~t∣t⊤X~t∣t−1+X~t∣t−1⊤X~t∣tNE−1,(1 - \alpha)^2 \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{x \mid y} + \alpha^2 \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x + \alpha (1 - \alpha) \frac{\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}^\top \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t-1} + \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t-1}^\top \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}}{N_\mathcal{E} - 1},(1−α)2Σ^x∣y​+α2Σ^x​+α(1−α)NE​−1X~t∣t⊤​X~t∣t−1​+X~t∣t−1⊤​X~t∣t​​,
(12.7)

so it mixes the correlations of forecast and analysis, and partly undoes the correlation information the observations provided. Members keep their identity through (12.6), and α=1\alpha = 1α=1 gives back the forecast anomalies exactly. At α=1\alpha = 1α=1 RTPS gives back the forecast spread but not the forecast members.

The two coincide when the analysis is an exact rescaling X~t∣t=aX~t∣t−1\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t} = a \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t-1}X~t∣t​=aX~t∣t−1​, since both then give ((1−α)a+α)X~t∣t−1((1 - \alpha) a + \alpha) \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t-1}((1−α)a+α)X~t∣t−1​. Any real analysis reshapes the anomalies, and then they differ.

Additive inflation¶

When a direction carries no spread at all, nothing that multiplies anomalies can help. Additive inflation Hamill & Whitaker, 2005 adds noise with its own covariance Ση∈RDx×Dx\gmat{\Sigma}_\eta \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}Ση​∈RDx​×Dx​, the covariance of the unrepresented model error:

x(e)←x(e)+η(e)−ηˉ,η(e)∼N(0,Ση).\vect{x}^{(e)} \leftarrow \vect{x}^{(e)} + \gvect{\eta}^{(e)} - \bar{\gvect{\eta}}, \qquad \gvect{\eta}^{(e)} \sim \mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta).x(e)←x(e)+η(e)−ηˉ​,η(e)∼N(0,Ση​).
(12.8)

inflate_additive subtracts the sample mean of the draws, so the ensemble mean is exactly preserved. The Bessel divisor makes that centring unbiased: E[(η(e)−ηˉ)(η(e)−ηˉ)⊤]=(1−1/NE)Ση\mathbb{E}[(\gvect{\eta}^{(e)} - \bar{\gvect{\eta}})(\gvect{\eta}^{(e)} - \bar{\gvect{\eta}})^\top] = (1 - 1 / N_\mathcal{E}) \gmat{\Sigma}_\etaE[(η(e)−ηˉ​)(η(e)−ηˉ​)⊤]=(1−1/NE​)Ση​, and summing over members and dividing by NE−1N_\mathcal{E} - 1NE​−1 leaves Ση\gmat{\Sigma}_\etaΣη​. So Σ^x\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_xΣ^x​ grows by Ση\gmat{\Sigma}_\etaΣη​ in expectation. It samples through perturbed_observations, so a diagonal Ση\gmat{\Sigma}_\etaΣη​ is never formed as a matrix.

Adaptive inflation¶

Hand-tuning ζ\zetaζ is awkward when the innovations themselves say whether the filter is over- or underdispersive. inflate_adaptive holds a Gaussian belief ζ∼N(μζ,σζ2)\zeta \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\zeta, \sigma_\zeta^2)ζ∼N(μζ​,σζ2​) and updates it each window. It is a simplified form of the scheme of Anderson (2009), with one global scalar and a fixed likelihood variance.

With the innovation rˉ∈RDy\bar{\vect{r}} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}rˉ∈RDy​ and its covariance Σ^y∈RDy×Dy\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_y}Σ^y​∈RDy​×Dy​ (chapter 13), the data-implied value is the clipped consistency statistic,

ζ^obs=clip(rˉ⊤Σ^y−1rˉDy,ζmin,ζmax),\hat{\zeta}_\text{obs} = \op{clip}\left(\frac{\bar{\vect{r}}^\top \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1} \bar{\vect{r}}}{D_y}, \zeta_\text{min}, \zeta_\text{max}\right),ζ^​obs​=clip⎝⎛​Dy​rˉ⊤Σ^y−1​rˉ​,ζmin​,ζmax​⎠⎞​,
(12.9)

with defaults ζmin=1\zeta_\text{min} = 1ζmin​=1 and ζmax=1.2\zeta_\text{max} = 1.2ζmax​=1.2. Under correct specification E[χ2/Dy]=1\mathbb{E}[\chi^2 / D_y] = 1E[χ2/Dy​]=1, with variance σobs2=2/Dy\sigma_\text{obs}^2 = 2 / D_yσobs2​=2/Dy​, which the code uses as the likelihood variance. The posterior is the Gaussian product,

μζ←σζ2ζ^obs+σobs2μζσζ2+σobs2,σζ2←σζ2σobs2σζ2+σobs2.\mu_\zeta \leftarrow \frac{\sigma_\zeta^2 \hat{\zeta}_\text{obs} + \sigma_\text{obs}^2 \mu_\zeta}{\sigma_\zeta^2 + \sigma_\text{obs}^2}, \qquad \sigma_\zeta^2 \leftarrow \frac{\sigma_\zeta^2 \sigma_\text{obs}^2}{\sigma_\zeta^2 + \sigma_\text{obs}^2}.μζ​←σζ2​+σobs2​σζ2​ζ^​obs​+σobs2​μζ​​,σζ2​←σζ2​+σobs2​σζ2​σobs2​​.
(12.10)

Two consequences follow by hand. The precision only ever grows, by Dy/2D_y / 2Dy​/2 per window:

1σζ,T2=1σζ,02+TDy2.\frac{1}{\sigma_{\zeta, T}^2} = \frac{1}{\sigma_{\zeta, 0}^2} + \frac{T D_y}{2}.σζ,T2​1​=σζ,02​1​+2TDy​​.
(12.11)

So μζ\mu_\zetaμζ​ becomes a running average of ζ^obs\hat{\zeta}_\text{obs}ζ^​obs​ over the whole history, and there is no forgetting.

The statistic also measures a different thing from the factor it is used as. If the true forecast variance is ζ2σ2\zeta^2 \sigma^2ζ2σ2 and the ensemble reports σ2\sigma^2σ2, then for one component E[χ2/Dy]=(ζ2σ2+σε2)/(σ2+σε2)\mathbb{E}[\chi^2 / D_y] = (\zeta^2 \sigma^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2) / (\sigma^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2)E[χ2/Dy​]=(ζ2σ2+σε2​)/(σ2+σε2​). That approaches ζ2\zeta^2ζ2 for precise observations and 1 for poor ones, and neither limit is ζ\zetaζ.

The first line prints 1.034884 1.034884 0.046512 0.046512, so one update matches the Gaussian product by hand. The three runs of 2,000 windows, starting from μζ=1\mu_\zeta = 1μζ​=1 and σζ2=0.05\sigma_\zeta^2 = 0.05σζ2​=0.05, end as follows:

The closed form (12.11) prints 1.0e-04, matching all three. A healthy filter ends above 1 because the clip keeps every excursion above 1 and removes those below it, so the estimate is biased upwards. The underdispersive run sits at the clip, however large the true deficit. The regime change ends between the two, since by then a new window has a weight of only about 5×10−45 \times 10^{-4}5×10−4 in (12.10). Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage¶

Rather than inflate the ensemble, one can regularise the covariance estimate Ledoit & Wolf, 2004. Shrinkage replaces Σ^x\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_xΣ^x​ by a convex combination with a scaled identity,

Σ^λ=(1−λ)Σ^x+λτI,τ=tr(Σ^x)Dx,\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\lambda = (1 - \lambda) \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x + \lambda \tau \mat{I}, \qquad \tau = \frac{\op{tr}(\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x)}{D_x},Σ^λ​=(1−λ)Σ^x​+λτI,τ=Dx​tr(Σ^x​)​,
(12.12)

with Σ^λ∈RDx×Dx\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}Σ^λ​∈RDx​×Dx​, τ\tauτ the average sample eigenvalue, and the intensity chosen to minimise the expected squared Frobenius distance to the truth:

λ=min⁡(1,b2d2),d2=∥Σ^x−τI∥F2,b2=1NE2∑e∥x~(e)x~(e)⊤−Σ^x∥F2.\lambda = \min\left(1, \frac{b^2}{d^2}\right), \qquad d^2 = \Vert \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x - \tau \mat{I} \Vert_F^2, \qquad b^2 = \frac{1}{N_\mathcal{E}^2} \sum_e \Vert \tilde{\vect{x}}^{(e)} \tilde{\vect{x}}^{(e) \top} - \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x \Vert_F^2.λ=min(1,d2b2​),d2=∥Σ^x​−τI∥F2​,b2=NE2​1​e∑​∥x~(e)x~(e)⊤−Σ^x​∥F2​.
(12.13)

Here d2d^2d2 measures how far the sample covariance is from the target, and b2b^2b2 how far it is from itself under sampling. The sample covariance uses the Bessel divisor, whereas Ledoit & Wolf (2004) use 1/NE1 / N_\mathcal{E}1/NE​, which is a small difference.

Three properties follow directly. The trace is unchanged, tr(Σ^λ)=tr(Σ^x)\op{tr}(\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\lambda) = \op{tr}(\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x)tr(Σ^λ​)=tr(Σ^x​), so shrinkage moves variance between directions and adds none, which is why it is not inflation. The smallest eigenvalue is at least λτ\lambda \tauλτ, so the result is positive definite whenever λτ>0\lambda \tau > 0λτ>0, however few members there are. And λ\lambdaλ is scale-invariant: multiplying the ensemble by aaa multiplies both b2b^2b2 and d2d^2d2 by a4a^4a4.

Computing it without squaring the units¶

Everything comes from the NE×NEN_\mathcal{E} \times N_\mathcal{E}NE​×NE​ Gram matrix KX~X~=X~X~⊤\mat{K}_{\tilde{X} \tilde{X}} = \tilde{\mat{X}} \tilde{\mat{X}}^\topKX~X~​=X~X~⊤, with no Dx×DxD_x \times D_xDx​×Dx​ array, at O(NE2Dx)O(N_\mathcal{E}^2 D_x)O(NE2​Dx​). With c=NE−1c = N_\mathcal{E} - 1c=NE​−1, as in the earlier chapters,

tr(Σ^x)=1ctr(KX~X~),∥Σ^x∥F2=1c2∥KX~X~∥F2,b2=1NE2(∑e[KX~X~]ee2+(NEc2−2c)∥KX~X~∥F2).\op{tr}(\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x) = \frac{1}{c} \op{tr}(\mat{K}_{\tilde{X} \tilde{X}}), \qquad \Vert \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x \Vert_F^2 = \frac{1}{c^2} \Vert \mat{K}_{\tilde{X} \tilde{X}} \Vert_F^2, \qquad b^2 = \frac{1}{N_\mathcal{E}^2} \left(\sum_e [\mat{K}_{\tilde{X} \tilde{X}}]_{ee}^2 + \left(\frac{N_\mathcal{E}}{c^2} - \frac{2}{c}\right) \Vert \mat{K}_{\tilde{X} \tilde{X}} \Vert_F^2\right).tr(Σ^x​)=c1​tr(KX~X~​),∥Σ^x​∥F2​=c21​∥KX~X~​∥F2​,b2=NE2​1​(e∑​[KX~X~​]ee2​+(c2NE​​−c2​)∥KX~X~​∥F2​).
(12.14)

The formula for b2b^2b2 comes from expanding the norm and using tr(X~Σ^xX~⊤)=∥KX~X~∥F2/c\op{tr}(\tilde{\mat{X}} \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x \tilde{\mat{X}}^\top) = \Vert \mat{K}_{\tilde{X} \tilde{X}} \Vert_F^2 / ctr(X~Σ^x​X~⊤)=∥KX~X~​∥F2​/c. But both b2b^2b2 and d2d^2d2 hold the fourth power of the anomalies, which leaves the float32 range for quite ordinary units. So gaussx first divides the factor by its largest entry, computes λ\lambdaλ from the unit-scale factor, and restores the scale only in τ\tauτ. That makes the computed λ\lambdaλ scale-invariant too, as the mathematics says it should be. Program 12.6 measures this, along with the properties above.

The first lines print 0.140867 0.140867, 40.589968 40.589968 and 0.190593 0.190593. So λ\lambdaλ matches its definition, the trace is preserved, and the smallest eigenvalue equals λτ\lambda \tauλτ exactly, because with NE<DxN_\mathcal{E} < D_xNE​<Dx​ the sample covariance is singular. The next line prints 14.92 18.80, so shrinkage lowers the Frobenius error against the true covariance on this draw. The line after prints LowRankUpdate 0e+00, since gaussx returns the same matrix as an operator that solves through Woodbury, and filterax.ledoit_wolf_shrinkage calls as_matrix on it.

In float32 the block prints:

Ensemble scaleledoit_wolf_shrinkageDefinition without rescaling
10-120.14087nan
10.140870.14087
10120.14087nan

Without rescaling, the fourth powers underflow at the small scale and overflow at the large one, and λ\lambdaλ comes out nan. The small scale is not exotic: a trace gas at parts per trillion has mole fractions of that order.

inflate_* act on the ensemble, and the next forecast sees the result. ledoit_wolf_shrinkage returns a matrix, and no filter consumes it for you. So it suits a parameter-space ensemble (chapter 9) or any computation that needs a well-conditioned covariance.

Implementation in filterax¶

LayerOffersNotes
Primitiveinflate_multiplicative, inflate_rtps, inflate_rtppcall gaussx, and are differentiable in the coefficient
Primitiveinflate_additive(key, particles, noise_cov)draws through perturbed_observations, then centres
Primitiveinflate_adaptivereturns the belief (μζ,σζ2)(\mu_\zeta, \sigma_\zeta^2)(μζ​,σζ2​), and inflates nothing itself
Primitiveledoit_wolf_shrinkagedense (Σ^λ,λ)(\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\lambda, \lambda)(Σ^λ​,λ); gaussx.ledoit_wolf_shrinkage returns the operator
ModuleMultiplicativeInflator, RTPS, RTPP, AdditiveInflatorAbstractInflator wrappers for the Layer 2 inflator= slot

The Layer 2 loop of chapter 16 runs forecast, analysis and then inflate. The inflator receives the analysis and the forecast, so this is posterior inflation, and analysis_history holds the ensemble after inflation. RTPS and RTPP raise ValueError without a forecast ensemble.

AdditiveInflator receives step= from the loop and folds it into its base_key, so windows draw independently. Called by hand with neither step nor key, it repeats one draw, as Program 12.4 prints. It is the one stochastic inflator, and differentiable_assimilate rejects it (chapter 14).

The coefficient of each module is a static field, so eqx.filter_grad cannot train it. To learn a factor, call the pure function with an array, as Program 12.8 does. inflate_adaptive has no module and the loop has no slot for it, so a run that uses it writes its own cycle.

Numerics¶

Mean preservation and the closed forms are exact to round-off, as Program 12.3 prints, and ordinary spreads present no float32 difficulty. Two details do matter, both in RTPS.

The floor ϵ\epsilonϵ in (12.5) is absolute, so RTPS is not scale-invariant at spreads near 10-12, unlike the shrinkage above. And jnp.std has an infinite slope at zero spread, so differentiating through RTPS with respect to the members gives NaN on a collapsed component.

It prints 2.000 and 1.000: the RTPS output spread in units of the small scale, where the forecast spread is 2. At unit scale the output is right. At a spread of 10-12 the floor equals the analysis spread, so κ=1\kappa = 1κ=1 and nothing is restored. The next line prints True, since the gradient holds NaN, so a differentiable run with RTPS needs no component collapsed exactly to zero. The line after prints 48.000, which is 2ζ∑e∥x~(e)∥22 \zeta \sum_e \Vert \tilde{\vect{x}}^{(e)} \Vert^22ζ∑e​∥x~(e)∥2 at ζ=1.5\zeta = 1.5ζ=1.5, so the pure function is differentiable in its factor. The last prints 0, since the module carries its coefficient as static data with no array leaf for eqx.filter_grad to find.

When it breaks¶

Program 12.9 shows the classic failure of uniform inflation, with no dynamics to bound the spread. It prints [ 0.32 0.32 145.123 146.375] for multiplicative inflation and [0.14 0.143 1.129 1.121] for RTPS. Under ζ=1.05\zeta = 1.05ζ=1.05 the two unobserved components grow by that factor in every window, and reach about 145 after 100 windows. Under RTPS they stay near their starting spread, since the analysis hardly contracted them and there is nothing to restore. In a chaotic system the attractor bounds this growth, but spread in a data-void region still grows until it does.

The other limits, each measured above:

  • Too much relaxation is as bad as too little: RTPS at α=0.8\alpha = 0.8α=0.8 returns nan in Program 12.7.

  • RTPP at α=0.5\alpha = 0.5α=0.5 gives an RMSE of 2.81 at NE=20N_\mathcal{E} = 20NE​=20, where ζ=1.02\zeta = 1.02ζ=1.02 gives 0.35.

  • Multiplicative inflation and RTPS cannot revive a collapsed direction, as Program 12.4 shows.

  • RTPP needs a forecast with spread in that direction, and only additive noise creates spread from nothing.

  • Additive noise adds error along with spread: its draws ignore the dynamics, and in Program 12.7 it gives 0.82 where ζ=1.02\zeta = 1.02ζ=1.02 gives 0.35.

  • An adaptive belief freezes, and with the default clip it cannot see an overdispersive filter at all, by (12.9) and Program 12.5.

  • Shrinkage lowers the Frobenius error of one covariance, and it adds neither members nor spread.

When inflation is the right answer¶

Almost always, in cycling, since every filter in this library loses spread for the reasons at the head of this chapter. A small constant inflation is the first thing to try. Use MultiplicativeInflator when coverage is roughly even and you want a single, cheap, differentiable knob. Use RTPS when coverage is uneven, since it inflates only what the analysis contracted and it keeps the correlations. Use RTPP when the analysis is suspected of damaging cross-variable relations and you can afford to give back part of the observations’ correlation information. Use AdditiveInflator when you have an estimate of model error and spread is missing in directions the ensemble does not span. Use inflate_adaptive for a slowly varying system, where a long running average is the wanted behaviour. Use ledoit_wolf_shrinkage when you need one well-conditioned covariance matrix, not a better ensemble.
